title: AWS CWI Exam Prep in New York, NY: 6-Day Course
description: Six-day AWS CWI exam prep for New York welding and special inspectors: DOB welding inspection rules, D1.1 and D1.5, Parts A, B and C, online or on site.
h1: AWS CWI Exam Prep in New York City: Six Days of Preparation for Special Inspection, Bridge and Shop Welding Inspectors
html:
In New York City, welding inspection is not just good practice; on most significant building work it is a regulated role with named qualifications. The Department of Buildings ties structural welding special inspection to specific credentials, and the AWS Certified Welding Inspector is the one that appears again and again. Add the city's bridges, its high-pressure steam and gas piping, and the steel fabricators across the Hudson and upstate who supply it all, and the CWI becomes a practical requirement for a large share of welding inspection jobs in the metro area. Atlantis NDT offers a six-day (6-day) course that prepares candidates for the AWS CWI examination. The American Welding Society owns the exam, sets who may sit it and issues the CWI; Atlantis provides the study and practice. For pricing, contact us about New York CWI exam prep.

What the course covers, and how New Yorkers take it

The six days follow the three parts of the AWS exam: two days on Fundamentals, one on the Part B practical, one on code application in the book you choose for Part C, one day of timed practice papers, and a closing day that revisits whatever the mock papers exposed and walks through exam-day logistics. The national CWI exam prep page sets out each day.

A candidate preparing alone gets the material online, with a study plan, notes, an original bank of practice items and an instructor who answers written questions. That suits inspectors who already work long site hours and need to study at odd times. A special inspection agency, fabricator or contractor can instead have the six days delivered at its own premises for a group. Atlantis has no office or classroom in New York, and the course is not run to a timetable. AWS has not endorsed the course, and none of its practice material comes from AWS exams.

What the Department of Buildings asks of welding inspectors

Under the city's special inspection framework, an owner hires a Special Inspection Agency registered with the Department of Buildings to perform the inspections the code requires, and the Department publishes a qualifications table for each category of work. The structural steel welding category covers welding of steel and aluminum and also high-pressure steam and gas piping and high-temperature hot water piping. The version of the table on the Department's site reads as follows:

Role in the agencyQualification route in the DOB table
Primary inspector or inspection supervisorA New York-licensed professional engineer or registered architect who holds the AWS CWI; or a PE or RA with the ICC Structural Welding Inspector certification and one year of relevant experience
Supplemental inspectorAn AWS CWI or ICC Structural Welding Inspector with three years of relevant experience
Supplemental inspector, restrictedAn AWS Certified Associate Welding Inspector, permitted to inspect only while a CWI or ICC Structural Welding Inspector is on site supervising

Two things follow for anyone planning a career here. First, the CWI is the common thread: it qualifies a technician as a supplemental inspector once the experience is there, and it is what a licensed engineer or architect pairs with the license to supervise welding inspection. Second, the CAWI is a real but limited entry point, useful for building experience under supervision. The Department updates its rules, so read the current table and rules on nyc.gov before relying on any one requirement.

Where the welding is: towers, bridges and building piping

High-rise and institutional steel

Steel-framed towers, hospital additions, university buildings, transit-oriented development and large residential projects keep structural steel erection going across the five boroughs. Field welding on those frames, from moment connections to column splices and deck attachments, is done to AWS D1.1 and inspected by the agency's welding inspectors against the approved drawings and the code. A typical day means confirming welder qualification cards, checking fit-up and preheat before welding starts in cold weather, watching technique on critical joints and writing up rejected welds for repair.

Bridges owned by the city, the MTA and the Port Authority

The New York City Department of Transportation looks after the East River crossings, including the Brooklyn, Manhattan, Williamsburg and Queensboro bridges, along with hundreds of smaller spans. MTA Bridges and Tunnels runs crossings such as the Verrazzano-Narrows, and the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey operates the George Washington Bridge and the Staten Island crossings. Rehabilitation and repair welding on steel bridges follows AWS D1.5, the bridge welding code, and owner specifications, with fracture-critical members held to tighter controls. Contractors and inspection consultants on that work need certified welding inspectors, and the bridge code is a Part C option.

High-pressure steam, gas and hot water piping

The same DOB welding category reaches inside buildings to high-pressure steam and gas piping and high-temperature hot water piping. Mechanical contractors installing or replacing that pipe weld to ASME qualifications, and the agency's welding inspector checks it. For an inspector who came up through the pipe trades, this is natural territory, and the ASME book on Part C fits it.

Transit, tunnels and utility infrastructure

The subway system, commuter rail yards, airport expansions and the utility networks under the streets all involve welded steel: station structures, platform and canopy framing, rail and equipment supports, and the large-diameter pipe and vaults of water, steam and gas systems. Owners on this kind of public work write their own specifications, usually referencing AWS D1.1 for structural welding and ASME or AWWA documents for pipe, and they staff resident inspection with consultants who need credentialed welding inspectors. Night and weekend work is normal because of track and traffic outages, which is another reason flexible online study suits people in this sector.

Waterfront and marine work

The harbor keeps ferries, tugs, barges and piers in constant need of repair. Pier rehabilitation means welding on steel piles, fender systems and bulkheads, often in tidal conditions where fit-up and moisture control are hard. Vessel repair follows owner and class requirements. A CWI brings a recognized standard of visual acceptance and record keeping to work that is otherwise judged by experience alone.

The shops that supply the city

Very little structural steel is fabricated inside the five boroughs. Girders, columns, trusses and bridge members come from shops in New Jersey, Pennsylvania, upstate New York and New England. Those fabricators run their own quality control, and many work under fabricator certification programs and owner specifications that expect qualified welding inspection personnel in the shop. Shop QC inspectors check incoming material, monitor procedures, measure finished welds and coordinate ultrasonic testing of complete-joint-penetration groove welds before members ship. Many New York-area CWIs start in one of these shops and later move to field special inspection, or the other way round.

The AWS New York and Long Island Sections

AWS District 2 includes two sections serving the metro area: the New York Section and the Long Island Section. Sections bring together welding engineers, inspectors, instructors, contractors, suppliers and students through meetings, technical talks and scholarship programs. A candidate gains three things by showing up. You meet CWIs working in special inspection and shop QC who will tell you how the job actually runs in this city. You find people senior enough to confirm your welding-related experience, which AWS asks you to document. And you hear which agencies and fabricators are hiring before the openings circulate. Contact details for both sections are on aws.org.

How New Yorkers learn the trade before they inspect it

Many of the city's welders come through union apprenticeships. Structural ironworkers, steamfitters and boilermakers all run multi-year programs that combine classroom hours with paid work, and the ironworker locals that cover Manhattan and the outer boroughs train a large share of the city's structural welders. Private trade schools in Queens and elsewhere also teach welding to people who want a faster start. For the CWI, formal training matters in two ways. AWS treats recognized trade or vocational courses, associate degrees and welding-related engineering study as education that shortens the experience requirement, so keep your apprenticeship records and school transcripts. And an apprenticeship's structured work history is exactly the kind of verifiable experience AWS wants to see.

Sitting the AWS exam from the five boroughs

Once AWS accepts your application, your confirmation letter carries an eligibility code. You use it to book Parts A and C, which are computer-based, at a Prometric center; AWS counts more than one hundred Prometric centers in the United States, and the New York metro area is well served, so pick whichever is easiest to reach by transit. The hands-on Part B is different: AWS stages it only where it holds a seminar and exam session, on dates it fixes, and US applicants have to be in about six weeks beforehand. Check the AWS seminar and exam schedule before choosing a month, because Part B may mean a trip out of state.

On the day, Part A means 150 questions, Part B means hands-on tasks with AWS-supplied tools and specimens plus 46 questions, and Part C means an open-book paper of roughly 50 to 65 questions in your chosen code. The pass mark AWS publishes is 72% on each part, and the clock at Prometric stops at two hours for either computer-based paper. AWS fee information is published on aws.org; see the CWI cost planning guide to budget the full process.

Part C choices for New York work

Pick the code you will actually use. Field special inspectors and shop QC staff on buildings take AWS D1.1; bridge inspectors and fabricators take AWS D1.5; inspectors on building steam and gas lines usually take the ASME book, where welding qualification under Section IX meets the power and process piping rules. Curtain-wall and architectural metal people sometimes take AWS D1.2 for aluminum. AWS also lists API 1104, AWS D15.1, AWS D17.1 and an ISO choice. Buy the edition printed on your AWS paperwork; it is not always the newest one in the shops.

For agencies and fabricators: the six days on your premises

Special inspection agencies and fabrication shops often need several people qualified at once, whether to staff a new contract or to move CAWIs and junior technicians up. On-site delivery suits that. The practical day uses your own gauges and real weld samples, and the code day can run in D1.1 or D1.5 to match your work, with exercises built around the kinds of nonconformance reports your inspectors write. Every person still applies to AWS individually and supplies their own experience record and vision examination; an employer cannot apply for them.

Eligibility, eyesight and the CAWI step

AWS balances schooling against welding-related work experience. With a high school diploma you need five years in welding-related work. A welding engineering or welding technology bachelor's brings that down to one year, while candidates who left school early need considerably longer. Separately, an eye examination recorded on the AWS form must show adequate near vision and color perception, and it must fall within the window AWS sets before your exam. Candidates who do not yet have the experience for the CWI can look at the CAWI, which in New York special inspection works under a CWI's supervision as described above. The CWI requirements guide covers both.

After the CWI

AWS keeps the CWI valid for nine years, with renewal filings at the three-year and six-year marks. In New York the credential opens several paths: supplemental inspector at a special inspection agency once the experience requirement is met, supervising inspector for those who also hold an engineering or architecture license, shop QC leadership, or the Senior CWI. Many inspectors also add nondestructive testing, since complete-joint-penetration welds on major frames and bridges are routinely tested ultrasonically. Under ASNT SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies NDT personnel after training and experience; Atlantis provides SNT-TC-1A-based training, described on NDT training in New York and VT Level 1 training. For the inspection side, see inspection services in New York and ultrasonic weld inspection.

Nearby CWI pages and requesting a quote

Candidates along the Northeast corridor can also read the CWI exam prep pages for Philadelphia, Boston and Baltimore.

To get a price, let us know the number of candidates, a sentence on each person's education and welding background, whether they lean toward D1.1, D1.5 or another book, and, for delivery on your premises, the address and the gauges and weld samples you can provide. Write to us through the New York CWI quote request and we reply within one business day.

faq.q: Does New York City require a CWI for structural welding inspection?
faq.a: The DOB qualifications table names the AWS CWI or the ICC Structural Welding Inspector for supplemental welding inspectors (with three years of experience), and a licensed PE or RA holding one of them for the primary inspector or supervisor. Check the current table and rules on nyc.gov.

faq.q: Can a CAWI work as a welding special inspector in New York?
faq.a: The DOB table allows an AWS Certified Associate Welding Inspector to inspect only while a CWI or ICC Structural Welding Inspector is on site supervising. It is a way to gain experience toward the CWI.

faq.q: Is there an Atlantis CWI class in Manhattan?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no New York classroom. Individuals study the six-day course online with written instructor support, and agencies or fabricators can host the six days at their own premises. Course outline.
The American Welding Society sets eligibility, administers all three parts and issues the CWI. The Atlantis course is preparation and carries no AWS approval or endorsement.

faq.q: Which code book should a New York bridge inspector choose?
faq.a: Go with D1.5. It governs steel bridge welding and is on the AWS list of Part C books. Building special inspectors usually choose D1.1. See AWS D1.5.

faq.q: Where do New York candidates sit the exam?
faq.a: The computer-based papers, Parts A and C, are booked at a Prometric center with the eligibility code from AWS. Part B is given by AWS at its seminar and exam sites on fixed dates, which may mean travel.

faq.q: Does my ironworker or steamfitter apprenticeship count toward eligibility?
faq.a: Recognized trade training can count on the education side of the AWS table, and the documented work hours help prove experience. AWS decides how your records are classed, so keep certificates and pay records.

faq.q: Can our special inspection agency have the six days on site?
faq.a: Yes. The practical and code days use your gauges, samples and code, and each person applies to AWS personally. Request a quote.

faq.q: Are the practice questions from past AWS exams?
faq.a: No. Every item is original, written by Atlantis to the subject areas AWS publishes; Atlantis never sees the live exam. Free method quizzes are on the NDT practice tests page.

faq.q: Should a New York CWI also learn ultrasonic testing?
faq.a: Complete-joint-penetration welds on major frames and bridges are commonly tested ultrasonically, so UT widens your role. Certification under SNT-TC-1A comes from the company that employs you once you have the method hours and training. See NDT training in New York.
